title: European Beech: Ancient Beeches You Can Visit
meta_description: Almost nothing grows under a beech, and the tree does that on purpose. Denmark's Svalebøgen is 12.5 metres round, several trunks fused into one.
intro: Almost nothing grows under a beech, and the tree is doing it deliberately. The leaves sit in dense overlapping layers that let very little light through, which is why a beech wood feels like a room rather than a thicket, and why left alone most of northern Europe would return to beech forest within two centuries. So a beech in a city park is often the one tree that would have been there anyway, which is what Nuremberg says of its two. The ones worth crossing town for are beeches given open ground, which keep their lower limbs and bring the crown down in a skirt you have to duck under. Prague's Twin Beech reaches 45 metres on a 1620 battlefield. Haarlem's carries a crowned monogram an exiled king cut into it around 1809. Denmark's Svalebøgen, said to have sprouted from a mouse's buried larder, is 12.5 metres round.
